source_read: PMC HTML (PMC4418947, author manuscript; Brain Res 2015;1628:174-185): abstract, unheaded two-paragraph Introduction, all eight headed body sections (structural imaging; structure and executive function; molecular imaging incl. monoamine systems, neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation, regional brain function; task fMRI; resting-state fMRI; implications for therapy), Figure 1-4 legends, highlights, acknowledgements, footnotes, and the bibliography entries needed to check citations (Volkow 2001a-d, Kim 2006, Salo 2009a/b, Simon 2010, Dean, Ersche 2012, Ballard 2014, Robertson 2013). Narrative review; no methods section, no tables.

claims.overstatement: None relative to this source; the claim is more cautious than the review's authors, who in places attribute the findings to methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity to dopamine terminals (Neuronal integrity section, para 1; Implications for Therapy, para 2), though hedged ('may in part be due to'). The review's own data (partial DAT recovery, inconsistent VMAT2, no human longitudinal D2 data) fit the claim's caution.
claims.note: Supported parts: lower striatal DAT is consistently reported (11-28%) and DAT partly recovers with abstinence. Not addressed in this source: the comparison with Parkinson's disease, and the explicit point that the measures cannot separate terminal loss from down-regulation (implied only by the recovery data). This is a narrative review by the UCLA group; numbers are second-hand.

anchors.locator: Molecular Imaging of Methamphetamine Users > Monoamine systems, para 2
anchors.extracted: Striatal DAT lower in abstinent users than matched non-users in PET studies with [11C]WIN-35,428 and [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate: deficits of 11-28% (Johanson 2006; McCann 1998, 2008; Sekine 2001; Volkow 2001b,d). Some participants abstinent up to 25 years (McCann 2008). TRODAT SPECT: up to 38% DAT recovery in the first 2 weeks of abstinence (5 users; Chou 2007). PET: DAT availability +19% caudate and +16% putamen between <6 months and 12-17 months of abstinence (5 people; Volkow 2001b as cited). DAT correlated with cognitive/psychomotor performance in some studies but not all.

VMAT2 findings inconsistent: [11C]DTBZ striatal binding higher in early abstinence (<3 weeks; +22% caudate, +12% putamen, +11% ventral striatum; Boileau 2008), differences diminishing with longer abstinence; another study 10% lower in users abstinent >3 months (Johanson 2006); a postmortem study found no striatal VMAT2 difference (Wilson 1996). SERT lower in users abstinent <1 year (Sekine 2006).

Striatal D2/D3 ([11C]raclopride) lower in users abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months: -16% caudate, -13% putamen, -8% nucleus accumbens; similar with [18F]fallypride at 4-10 days. Recovery of D2 shown in rodents and monkeys; no human longitudinal D2 studies.

anchors.locator: Neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation, para 1; Implications for Therapy, para 2
anchors.extracted: Authors frame findings in terms of neurotoxicity: cite 'mounting evidence' (reviews, largely animal) that repeated exposure can produce neurotoxicity; suggest poor response to dopamine agonists may in part reflect methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity to dopamine terminals. NAA/Cr in ACC appears to recover slowly with extended abstinence (Nordahl 2005; Salo 2011). No human terminal counts are cited.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement. The claim omits two qualifications this source gives: users also show LARGER striatal (and parietal) grey-matter volumes than non-users in several studies, and cortical grey matter increased over the first month of abstinence in one study (Morales 2012; uncorrected threshold).
claims.note: Supported here: smaller frontal (ACC, DLPFC, OFC), temporal, hippocampal and insular grey matter in users; smokers who did not use methamphetamine also had smaller OFC (and caudate) grey matter than non-smoking non-users (Morales 2012 as summarized). Not in this source: the '4 of 10' count, the failure to reproduce the 7.8% hippocampal finding, and the point about memory scores. Note the review says OFC and caudate, the claim says orbitofrontal only.

anchors.locator: Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, para 2
anchors.extracted: Users generally have smaller cortical but larger striatal grey-matter volumes than non-users (Berman 2008a). After <3 weeks abstinence: smaller ACC, DLPFC, OFC, superior temporal and hippocampal grey matter (Nakama 2011; Thompson 2004); insular grey-matter density deficit with abstinence up to 6 months (Schwartz 2010). Users abstinent 3-4 months: larger parietal, caudate, lenticular, accumbens, putamen and globus pallidus volumes (Jernigan 2005; Chang 2005).

Smoking 87-92% among methamphetamine users vs 22% of the general population. Morales 2012: smokers, with or without methamphetamine use, had smaller OFC and caudate grey matter than non-smoking non-users; users who smoked had smaller superior/inferior temporal, supramarginal and precentral grey matter than smokers who did not use methamphetamine. Authors: OFC and caudate deficits may be partly attributable to smoking or premorbid conditions.

anchors.locator: Structural Brain Imaging, para 3 and Figure 1 legend
anchors.extracted: Grey matter increased between weeks 1 and 4 of abstinence in inferior frontal, angular, superior temporal gyri, precuneus, insula and occipital pole (Morales 2012; map at p<0.005 uncorrected, cluster >200 voxels); no change in controls rescanned about 1 month apart. Users abstinent >=6 months had higher middle frontal grey-matter density than shorter abstinence (Kim 2006).

claims.overstatement: 'Indicates that some differences ... predate drug use' is a little stronger than the review, which says the findings 'suggest' some abnormalities 'may predate' use. A shared sibling trait shows familial (genetic or environmental) vulnerability, not that the same trait was present in the user before use.
claims.note: Supported: dependent participants and their non-using siblings shared larger putamen, amygdala and hippocampal volumes and lower fractional anisotropy than controls; only the dependent participants had smaller OFC and anterior insula; the authors infer some but not all differences may predate use. Not in this source: that siblings had poorer inhibitory control than controls (the review reports only that fractional anisotropy near the right IFG correlated with stop-signal performance across all three groups), effect sizes, and the cocaine-versus-methamphetamine composition (the review says only 'cocaine- or amphetamine-dependent').

anchors.extracted: Ersche 2012: 50 cocaine- or amphetamine-dependent individuals and their siblings without chronic drug use vs healthy controls. Dependent and siblings: larger putamen, amygdala and hippocampal grey matter than controls; only dependent: smaller OFC and anterior insula; both: lower fractional anisotropy. Review concludes some but not all structural abnormalities may predate use.

anchors.locator: Deficits in Brain Structure and Impaired Executive Functions, para 1
anchors.extracted: Fractional anisotropy in tracts near the right inferior frontal gyrus positively related to stop-signal inhibitory control in stimulant users, their siblings and controls (Ersche 2012). No group comparison of siblings' inhibitory performance is given.

reporting_issues.note: Bibliography: 2001a = Am J Psychiatry 158:2015-21 (D2/orbitofrontal); 2001b = J Neurosci 21:9414-8 (DAT recovery). The raclopride numbers are cited to 2001b; the Implications section correctly cites 2001a for D2 and prefrontal activity.

Only Kim SJ et al. 2006 (Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 9:221-8, prefrontal grey matter in short- and long-term abstinence) is listed. The grey-matter density and WCST attributions fit that paper; the fractional-anisotropy correlation and the prefrontal white-matter glucose finding do not.
Structural section para 5 says users have lower FA in the genu; executive-function section para 2 says Stroop/WCST deficits correlate with increased FA in the genu.

The paragraph's evidence is mixed rather than contrary. Two of its findings support the lead sentence: thalamic but not striatal metabolism increased at 12-17 months (Wang 2004), i.e. striatal values did not recover, and prefrontal white-matter metabolism was lower in users abstinent a mean 19 months (attributed to Kim 2006). Only the thalamic increase and the blood-flow comparison (introduced with 'Still') point to recovery. The lead sentence overstates persistence somewhat but is not contradicted by its evidence.

Checked against the Simon 2010 full text (read for this batch): significant user-control difference only on Stroop colours (processing speed); timed executive domain p=.09, untimed executive not significant; Stroop colours and composite non-significant with education as covariate.
Printed as F31 DA0331-17 alongside F31 DA033120-02.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 applied to a narrative review necessarily gives critically low; every critical item unmet.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One more element for 'claimed': the review frames the molecular findings causally in places ('mounting evidence' of neurotoxicity, Neuronal integrity para 1; poor agonist efficacy 'may in part be due to methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity to dopamine nerve terminals', Implications para 2) while reporting partial DAT recovery and inconsistent VMAT2 data.

missed: Causal neurotoxicity framing of the dopamine findings (Neuronal integrity and neuroinflammation, para 1; Implications for Therapy, para 2) is not recorded among key findings or in the interpretation gap; it matters for cl_meth_dopamine_damage, where this review is the source whose authors lean furthest toward terminal damage.

Larger striatal and parietal grey-matter volumes in users than non-users (Berman 2008a; Jernigan 2005; Chang 2005; Jan 2012b; Structural Brain Imaging, para 2) are not among the key findings; relevant to how cl_meth_grey_matter frames the structural literature as 'less grey matter'.

For cl_meth_siblings: the review gives no sibling-versus-control comparison of inhibitory control (only an FA-stop-signal correlation across all three groups; Deficits in Brain Structure, para 1) and does not give the cocaine/amphetamine split of the 50 dependent participants; those parts of the claim need the primary paper (Ersche 2012).

The Introduction (unheaded, 2nd paragraph) states that neuroimaging studies have 'demonstrated' that users typically display corticostriatal dysfunction; fits the card's substantial gap but is not quoted there.
